beats.text: Three processes are ready. There is one CPU. Who goes first?
Each needs the CPU for one stretch of work, its CPU burst. Here, twenty-four, three, and three milliseconds.
Two numbers judge a schedule. Turnaround time is when you finish, minus when you arrived.
Waiting time is turnaround minus your burst: the time you sat ready, but not running.
Arrive at two, need nine, finish at twenty-six. Turnaround, twenty-four. Waiting, fifteen.
The simplest rule is first come, first served. P one arrived first, so P one runs.
And runs. And runs. Twenty-four milliseconds. P two and P three only need three each, but they wait.
P two waits twenty-four. P three waits twenty-seven. The average waiting time is seventeen.
Short jobs stuck behind a long one. That is the convoy effect.
Now the same three arrive in a different order: P two, P three, then P one.
Waiting times six, zero and three. The average drops to three. Same work, same rule, very different result.
So why not always run the shortest job first?
That is S J F, shortest job first. Four processes need six, eight, seven, and three.
The shortest goes first: P four, then P one, then P three, then P two.
Waiting times three, sixteen, nine and zero. The average is seven, the lowest any order can give.
The catch: the OS cannot see the future. It does not know how long the next burst will be. It can only estimate it.
And a long job can starve, while short ones keep arriving.
Both rules are nonpreemptive. Once a process has the CPU, it keeps it until it finishes or blocks.
For the exam.
Draw the Gantt chart first.
Turnaround is completion minus arrival.
Waiting is turnaround minus burst.
FCFS suffers the convoy effect.
S J F: minimum average wait, unknown bursts.
